strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse tasks (mathematical reasoning, visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding) and multiple model sizes (1.5B and 7B), demonstrating broad applicability
Practical simplification of RL training by removing critic model, reference model, and KL constraints, reducing computational overhead and memory requirements
Consistent empirical improvements over GRPO across most benchmarks (2.6-9.6% gains), with particularly strong results on visual reasoning (9.64% on CV-Bench)
Clear methodology with useful ablations (group size sensitivity, reward normalization strategy, KL constraint analysis) providing insights into design choices
Well-motivated research questions about necessity of surrogate loss functions and potential for streamlined learning strategies
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is primarily component removal from GRPO; group-level reward normalization and standardization already exist in prior work
Weak theoretical justification: no analysis of why removing policy constraints doesn't harm performance; claims to 'directly optimize original objective' lack rigor and theoretical support
Modest empirical improvements without statistical significance analysis: 1.6-2.6% average gains lack error bars/confidence intervals and could be within noise margins; no multiple runs reported
Unfair hyperparameter comparison: paper acknowledges using GRPO's hyperparameters 'despite their suboptimality' for GPG; fair comparison requires separate tuning for both methods

Unexplained architectural change: Figure 3 shows GPG generates progressively shorter sequences, but paper provides no analysis of whether this indicates better reasoning or easier-to-get-right short answers; this affects fairness of accuracy comparisons
Incomplete component attribution: ablations don't isolate individual contributions (reference model vs KL vs clipping); cannot determine which removal contributes most to improvements
Limited baseline comparisons: primarily compares against GRPO only; Dr. GRPO appears in one table; missing comparisons with other recent simplification methods

Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable at review time despite claims; different codebases used (Open-r1, VisualThinker, R1-V, Visual-RFT) may introduce implementation divergence; Algorithm 1 lacks sufficient detail
Narrow experimental scope: evaluation limited to reasoning tasks only; generalization to other RL alignment objectives (general instruction following, dialogue) unknown
Method section lacks intuition: central equations (5-6) presented without explanation for design choices; no justification for per-token normalization approach

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse tasks (unimodal and multimodal) with consistent improvements over GRPO
Clear problem motivation and straightforward method explanation
Comprehensive ablation studies examining group size, reward normalization, and KL constraints
Implementation details provided with code promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is changing advantage estimation from value-function-based to group-normalized, which is an incremental modification rather than fundamental innovation
Unfair experimental comparison: authors explicitly used suboptimal hyperparameters for GPG while keeping GRPO's parameters, violating fair comparison principles
Completely unsupported central claim: paper claims 'significantly reducing computational costs' but provides zero measurements of training time, memory usage, or throughput

Lack of theoretical justification: no explanation for why removing policy constraints improves performance (contradicts RL theory); ablation shows KL constraints hurt performance but remains unexplained
Missing critical baselines and comparisons: only compares with GRPO as main baseline; minimal comparison with REINFORCE++, DAPO, ReMax, or proper tuning of Dr. GRPO
No statistical significance testing: results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; improvements often modest (1-3% average) without evidence of significance
Misleading framing: claims to 'directly optimize the original RL objective' but still uses advantage estimation (just different method); not fundamentally different from GRPO
Methodological concerns: group-level statistics may be unreliable with default group size of 8; sensitivity to group composition not thoroughly analyzed

Inconsistent improvements across tasks: performance gains vary from <1% to 10%, with sometimes worse performance on certain benchmarks (e.g., OlympiadBench), but no analysis of what determines success

Insufficient analysis and evidence: Figure 2 provides only anecdotal single example; Figure 3 shows different training dynamics but lacks interpretation; no explanation for why group normalization outperforms batch normalization (Table 10)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (1.5B-7B), diverse tasks (mathematical reasoning, visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding), and consistent improvements over GRPO
Clear motivation and well-articulated research questions about directly optimizing RL objectives without surrogate losses
Practical simplicity: eliminates critic models and reference models, reducing implementation complexity and potential computational overhead
Thorough ablation studies examining group size sensitivity, reward normalization strategies, and KL constraints
Clear presentation with good organization, intuitive figures, detailed comparison tables, and reproducibility commitment (code promised)
Effective across both unimodal and multimodal scenarios, demonstrating robustness and broad applicability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: method is essentially GRPO with KL divergence and reference model removed; group-level reward normalization is standard practice

Weak theoretical justification: claims to 'directly optimize original RL objective' but still uses policy gradient approximations; no explanation for why removing KL divergence helps; lacks convergence guarantees

No statistical rigor: absence of error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing for claimed improvements; cannot distinguish genuine gains from random variance with modest 1-3% improvements in many cases

Incomplete computational cost analysis: claims 'significantly reduces computational costs' but provides no wall-clock time comparisons, GPU memory measurements, or actual training efficiency metrics; Figure 3 shows smoother curves but doesn't quantify savings

Insufficient baseline comparisons: primarily compares against GRPO; limited comparison with PPO and other recent RL methods; Dr. GRPO only in Table 3; authors acknowledge using suboptimal GRPO hyperparameters, making it unclear if gains reflect method merit

Technical soundness concerns: no discussion of edge cases in group-wise normalization when std approaches zero; one-step advantage estimation justified as 'sufficiently effective' without rigorous justification; ablation shows monotonic improvement with group size up to 16 but lacks practical guidance
Limited model scale: all experiments ≤7B models; broader impact section acknowledges not evaluating on larger scales, limiting generalization claims
Counterintuitive finding unexplained: Table 10 shows adding KL constraint decreases performance, contradicting standard RL theory; deserves deeper investigation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across unimodal and multimodal tasks with multiple model sizes (1.5B, 7B) and extensive benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over GRPO baselines
Practical value through simplified training: eliminates reference model and critic, reduces memory usage (24G vs 28G), and lowers training cost (0.45× relative to DAPO)
Thorough ablation studies and analysis systematically showing the contribution of each component (Tables 1, 10, 11, 13, 15) and gradient bias visualization (Figure 2)
Clear identification and mathematical formulation of gradient estimation bias problem (Equation 7), with empirical validation across training
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, multiple framework implementations, multiple random seeds with standard deviations reported (Table 16), and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contributions are component removal and a mathematically trivial gradient bias correction (Equation 7). The method is still policy gradient with group-based advantages, not a fundamental algorithmic advance

Ad-hoc design choices lack principled justification: (1) removing Fnorm = std{R(o)} introduces reward bias but hurts performance, requiring ad-hoc α-scaling solution; (2) no explanation for why KL constraint is harmful (Table 13); (3) α = B/(B-M) varies across batches without convergence analysis

Experimental setup fairness concerns: GRPO uses reportedly suboptimal hyperparameters for comparison rather than being properly tuned; baseline reproductions show inconsistencies (Oat-Zero: 51.4% vs 47.8%); high variance in results (±8.8% in Table 16) makes claimed 1-3% improvements marginal

Incomplete analysis: no breakdown of performance gains from each component (removing reference model, removing KL, gradient correction, thresholding); limited comparison with concurrent methods (Dr. GRPO, REINFORCE++); general benchmark improvements are negligible (MMLU +0.22%, C-Eval +0.38%) with mixed per-dataset results

Theoretical gaps: no convergence guarantees or analysis of policy divergence without KL constraints; claim of directly optimizing original RL objective (Eq. 1) is misleading given biased advantage estimates; no justification for why specific α-scaling improves optimization beyond empirical observation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model scales (1.5B, 7B), diverse reasoning benchmarks (AIME24, MATH-500, AMC23, etc.), and multimodal tasks with consistent improvements over GRPO
Strong empirical results with proper reproducibility practices including multiple random seeds, detailed hyperparameter documentation, and promised code release
Practical value through computational efficiency gains (no critic/reference model) and consistent gains across nearly all evaluated tasks
Well-organized extensive ablation studies examining Fnorm, group size, AGE, thresholding, and reward normalization choices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contributions reduce to removing GRPO components (critic, reference model, KL divergence). The 'Accurate Gradient Estimation' (Eq. 7, α=B/(B-M)) is elementary statistics—a straightforward correction when some samples produce zero gradients—not a meaningful methodological advance

Weak theoretical justification: no analysis of why simplifications help; claims about 'directly optimizing the original RL objective' are misleading since Eq. 5 still uses advantage function approximation from finite samples like PPO/GRPO

Confounding variables in experiments: Table 1 reveals that with proper reward normalization (Fnorm=std{R(o)}), GPG achieves only 45.3% vs GRPO's 43.7%. Large improvements (48.3%) depend critically on multiple design choices (Fnorm=1, AGE, βth=0.6), making it unclear whether improvements stem from the simplified algorithm or extensive tuning

Ad-hoc design decisions lack principled justification: Fnorm=1 outperforms theoretically more sound Fnorm=std{R(o)} without explanation; thresholding mechanism contradicts simplicity claims; α scaling factor has no optimality justification; Table 13 shows KL constraints hurt performance but provides no explanation

Insufficient analysis of why the method works: Figure 2 shows α and reward std vary, but causal relationships to improvements are unclear; no explanation for why removing reference model helps beyond computational benefits; counterintuitive findings (Fnorm=1 working better) unexplained

Overstated novelty and significance: describing incremental simplifications as 'revisiting policy gradients' and claiming to 'directly optimize original RL objective' misleads about actual contributions; improvements are empirical but accompanied by numerous hyperparameters, undermining simplicity claims

Incomplete analysis and missing comparisons: limited exploration of hyperparameter sensitivity (βth only tested at 0.6, 0.8); minimal gains on general benchmarks (MMLU +0.22, C-Eval +0.38) suggest task-specific benefits; DAPO shows competitive performance contradicting efficiency claims

Experimental design issues: different datasets used for 7B comparisons (Yu et al., 2025) complicate fair comparison; reproduced GRPO numbers vary inconsistently across tables; no evaluation on larger models due to computational constraints

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple model sizes (1.5B, 7B), diverse datasets (AIME24, MATH-500, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench), and both unimodal and multimodal tasks with consistent improvements
Practical efficiency gains: achieves superior performance with 0.45× training cost, 0.39× data cost, and lower memory footprint than DAPO
Strong empirical results: 55.7% vs 48.9% on 1.5B models, 57.7% vs 46.6% on 7B, and significant multimodal improvements (76.15% vs 59.47% on CV-Bench)

Excellent reproducibility practices with detailed implementation details, algorithm specification, and commitment to release code; includes robustness evaluation with multiple random seeds and general capability assessment (MMLU, C-Eval)
Clear identification of practical issues in GRPO: reward bias in advantage functions and gradient estimation bias from invalid samples, with intuitive solutions
Well-motivated simplification approach for the LLM era where pretraining already provides strong representations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is primarily removing components from GRPO; AGE technique (Eq. 7) is straightforward gradient scaling (B/(B-M)), functioning more as a bug fix than novel method; Algorithm 1 is only 3 lines

Insufficient theoretical justification: no formal analysis explaining why removing constraints works better; claim of 'directly optimizing the original RL objective' is misleading since group-based normalization is still a form of baseline; why AGE specifically helps versus other gradient scaling approaches is unexplained

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Table 1 shows Fnorm=1, α=1 underperforms GRPO before AGE helps, but paper doesn't adequately explain this progression or why GRPO's normalization provides implicit gradient correction

Weak comparison with concurrent work: Dr. GRPO also analyzes reward bias and debiasing, but comparison is superficial; paper dismisses it as 'did not significantly outperform GRPO' without thorough analysis of why their approach is superior

Experimental design concerns: baseline inconsistency (Qwen2.5-Math-7B base at 30.9% vs Instruct at 43.8%), inconsistent reward functions across settings (accuracy-only for 7B vs additional rewards for multimodal), and limited justification for hyperparameter choices

Narrow generalization: primarily evaluated on math reasoning and vision tasks; minimal gains on general benchmarks (MMLU +0.22, C-Eval +0.38) suggest specialized effectiveness; acknowledged inability to evaluate on very large models due to computational constraints

Incomplete ablations: limited threshold sensitivity exploration (only βth=0.6 vs 0.8), missing analysis of when AGE helps most, no evaluation of diminishing returns with group size; large standard deviations in results (e.g., AIME24: 31.7±8.8) raise significance concerns

Presentation issues: claim of 'directly optimizing original RL objective' is overstated; dense presentation scatters results across multiple tables; limited case study evidence; insufficient discussion of failure cases or method limitations
